newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesian/Malaysian food imports seen rising.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian/Malaysian food imports seen rising.

text.p: Indonesia and Malaysia's food supplies are secure, but both countries will become more reliant on imports as eating habits change and domestic output fails to keep pace with population growth, officials said on Friday.

Indonesia, the world's fourth most populous nation with 200 million people, is taking bold steps to ensure food sufficiency, especially in rice, in a bid to keep a lid on imports amid a fast-changing national diet.

The government has launched a programme to cultivate rice in 640,000 hectares (1.6 million acres) in Central Kalimantan on Borneo Island, spending 500 billion rupiah ($212 million) just on irrigation systems and land clearing.
Indonesia has also embarked on a project to plant 500,000 hectares (1.24 million hectares) with hybrid corn.

"Imports are huge whenever we face supply side problems related to the weather, transporation and infrastructure," senior economist Miranda Gultom of the Coordinating Ministry for Economics, Finance and Development, told Reuters.
She said percapita rice consumption in Indonesia has been falling, with Indonesians showing more interest in wheat and corn products.
"Five years from now, Indonesians will be eating more corn flakes and corn chips and soybean," she added.
MALAYSIA HEAVILY DEPENDENT ON FOOD IMPORTS
Malaysian officials said there was a comfortable supply of food in the country, though most of it had to be imported.
The staple diet in this booming Southeast Asian nation of 20 million people, as elsewhere in the region, is rice.
Officials said about 450,000 tonnes of rice was imported in 1996, mostly from Thailand.
A flour shortage in June this year, sparked by high wheat prices in the U.S., has prompted grains importers to stock adequately on wheat until April 1997, grains dealers said.
Chicken consumption is estimated at about one million birds a year and supply was comfortable, poultry dealers said.
Production of raw sugar is estimated at around 90,000 tonnes yearly while consumption was 861,266 tonnes in 1995. Imports are sourced from Australia, Fiji and Thailand.
Officials said agricultural production has declined steadily since the mid-1980s, after the country shifted its focus to industrialisation from being an agricultural-based economy.
Agricultural output is only estimated to have grow by 1.4 percent in 1997 after the 1.6 percent in 1996 and 1.1 percent last year, the central Bank Negara Malaysia said in its annual economic report.
Agriculture's contribution to gross domestic product was forecast to have fallen to 12.7 percent in 1996 from 13.5 percent last year, Bank Negara said.
Officials said the government was concerned with the surging cost of food items, which has been a major reason for creeping inflation, and has encouraged farmers and food producers to boost output.
Revenue from the food, beverages and tobacco market was estimated at 11.92 million ringgit ($4.73 billion) in 1996, a decline of 10.7 percent from the 13.35 million ringgit generated in 1995.
